text:
Keep the Joined Up Hand

Every few years a headline announces the death of handwriting. Keyboards have won, the story goes, and children who will spend their working lives tapping on glass should not waste precious classroom hours looping their letters together. It is a tidy argument and it sounds modern. I think it is wrong. Primary schools should keep teaching joined up handwriting, and they should teach it properly, with time and patience, because it serves children in ways that typing cannot and because the case against it rests on a misunderstanding of what handwriting is for.

The first mistake is to treat handwriting as a delivery system for words, a slow and inferior cousin of the keyboard. If that were all it was, the critics would have a point. Nobody defends the abacus against the calculator on grounds of speed. But handwriting is not merely a way to get text onto a surface. It is a motor and cognitive skill that shapes how young children learn to read, spell and compose. Asking whether handwriting is faster than typing is like asking whether walking is faster than driving. The answer is obvious and it misses the reason we teach children to walk.

Consider the evidence on letter learning. Studies of young children, including work by Karin James and colleagues in the United States, have found that children who practise forming letters by hand show stronger activation in the brain regions linked to reading than children who type or trace the same letters. The messy variability of hand drawn letters appears to help. Each attempt is slightly different, so the child must work out what makes an a an a. A keyboard offers the same identical key every time. Nothing is wrong with the key, but it asks the brain for very little, and early childhood is exactly when the brain is most ready to be asked.

A fair critic will accept all this and still wonder why the letters must be joined. Print lettering is also handwriting. Why not stop there and move on to typing? The answer lies in what joining does to the movement. In print, the pen lifts after almost every letter, and each letter is a separate decision. In a joined hand, the pen travels through whole words in a single flowing motion. The child learns to think of a word as a unit, a rhythm with a shape. That matters for spelling, because common letter strings such as ing, tion and ough become motor habits as well as visual ones. Many teachers report that children who write these patterns fluidly misspell them less often, and it makes sense that the hand would remember what the eye forgets.

Then there is fluency. A child who must think about every letter shape has less attention left for the sentence, the argument and the story. Fluent handwriting frees working memory for composition, and research on young writers has repeatedly linked handwriting automaticity with the length and quality of their written work. A joined hand, once automatic, is also faster than print. That is why most adults who write quickly by hand drift towards some form of joining whether they were taught it or not. Notes in a meeting, a shopping list, a signature on a form, all come more easily from a hand that flows. Schools that skip joining do not remove the drift. They simply leave children to invent it badly, with odd shortcuts that nobody has checked for legibility.

There is also a matter of fairness. Households differ in how many devices they own and how often children touch a pencil outside school. If schools abandon handwriting instruction, the children who suffer most will be those whose homes offered the least practice. Affluent families will buy tutors, calligraphy sets and tablets with styluses. Others will rely on whatever the school provides. Handwriting is one of the rare skills that costs almost nothing to teach well. A pencil, a sheet of paper and ten focused minutes a day are enough. Dropping it saves very little and widens a gap that schools exist to narrow.

Practicality counts too. Pupils will sit handwritten examinations for years to come, and a child who cannot write legibly at speed will be penalised for something unrelated to understanding. Beyond school, people still fill in forms, sign documents, jot notes, write cards and labels, and take messages when the battery has died. Poor handwriting remains a mild social cost, and a clear confident script is a small credential that costs the school very little to confer. Teachers know the quiet unfairness here. Two pupils can give the same correct answer, yet the one whose writing is hard to read is marked down, or simply judged less capable, long before anyone checks the content. A school that withholds the training that prevents this is making a choice, even if it presents the choice as progress.

I want to be honest about the limits of the evidence. Some of the most quoted studies, such as those suggesting that students remember more when they take notes by hand, have been challenged on replication, and I do not rest my case on them. The research on letter learning is stronger, but it concerns handwriting in general and not joining in particular. My argument for joining is therefore partly an argument from craft and experience. It is built on how fluency develops, what teachers observe and what adults actually do once they write at speed. That is a reasonable basis for a school policy, though it should be tested as we go and not treated as settled.

The strongest objection concerns children for whom handwriting is a struggle. Some pupils with dyslexia, dyspraxia or motor difficulties find joined writing hard, and forcing it can sap their confidence. I take this seriously. But the answer is support and flexibility, not abolition. Some specialists argue that continuous movement actually helps certain dyslexic pupils, because it reduces reversals of letters like b and d, and that is one reason a number of specialist programmes favour it. Where a child truly cannot manage it, a school should offer alternatives without fuss, including a keyboard. A policy designed around the exceptions would deny the rule to everyone else.

Another objection is opportunity cost. The school day is crowded, and every minute spent on loops is a minute not spent on coding, or on typing. This sounds reasonable until the numbers are examined. A sound handwriting programme needs perhaps fifteen minutes a few times a week. Typing can be taught alongside it, and should be. The two skills are partners and not rivals. A child can learn to type with ten fingers and to write with a flowing hand, and the combination serves them better than either alone. Nobody argues that learning to ride a bicycle should be dropped because buses exist.

Finally, there is something that does not fit neatly into a study. Handwriting is personal. A joined hand carries a trace of the person who made it, which is why a handwritten letter lands differently from an email. Children who can write well, or even just competently, have access to that expressive channel. They can make a birthday card for a grandparent that ends up pinned to a fridge for a year. They can also read the cursive in old family letters, school registers and archives, which would otherwise become a locked language. A generation unable to read handwriting would be cut off from its own past in a small but real way.

If we keep it, we should do it well. Too often joined writing is taught late, hurriedly and without feedback, so children develop clumsy habits that stay for life. Better practice begins with posture and pencil grip in the early years, introduces letter families that share a movement, adds simple exit strokes early so that joining feels natural, and then gives short regular practice instead of occasional marathons. Teachers need training for this, because it is a craft and not simply something to be assigned. Once the basics are secure, pupils should be free to develop a personal style, since legibility and speed matter more than copying a model alphabet.

The sensible position is not nostalgia and it is not surrender. Nobody needs to pretend that keyboards are going away, and every child should leave primary school able to type. But the choice has never really been between pens and screens. It is between giving children one more way to think and communicate and giving them one fewer. Joined up handwriting trains the hand, supports reading and spelling, frees attention for ideas, narrows rather than widens gaps, and keeps open a door to the written past. It costs a few minutes a week. Schools should keep teaching it, and teach it well.
